Karl Landsteiner. The Austrian-American pathologist and immunologist who transformed transfusion medicine from a deadly gamble into a safe procedure through his discovery of the human ABO blood groups.

Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood group system in 1901, the landmark finding that human blood types could be classified by antigen-antibody reactions. This discovery single-handedly eliminated transfusion incompatibility deaths. He also identified the poliovirus in 1909, proving that a filterable infectious agent, too small for light microscopy to see, could cause disease. This vindicated the viral theory of infection and opened a new frontier in medicine.

Among his other key contributions was Landsteiner's rule, the principle that blood sera contain antibodies to antigens absent on the individual's own red cells. He pioneered laboratory methods for detecting and measuring immune responses, developing precipitation reactions and complement fixation techniques. These methods were rigorous and revolutionary for his time.

Landsteiner worked primarily in Vienna and later at the Rockefeller Institute in New York, where he conducted decades of methodical immunological experiments. In 1930, he won the Nobel Prize, one of the last recognitions for classical serology before molecular methods would eclipse this approach. His work with Paul Ehrlich in immunology complemented Ehrlich's theoretical framework of receptors. While Ehrlich theorized that receptors existed, Landsteiner experimentally verified immune specificity through antigen-antibody reactions, providing the proof that made immunity a science.
